newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Pace picks up, buyers firmly in control.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Pace picks up, buyers firmly in control.

text.p: Big-name investment banks get back in the initial public offering game this week after a long winter's nap and should rouse plenty of demand for new stock, but the overall market tone still belongs to buyers.

Coldwater Creek, Metro Information Services, and Administaff Inc. are the hottest of a batch of nearly 30 initial public offerings this week, IPO analysts say. The deals could rack up premiums of a dollar or more a share on their first day of trading.
"Next week, the big boys are back in town," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket, noting deals coming from Morgan Stanley Group Inc., Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc., and Smith Barney.

Direct mail catalog company Coldwater Creek sells clothing, gifts and jewelry. Its $35 million IPO will be lead managed by Montgomery Securities. The Sandpoint, Idaho, company has been profitable every year since fiscal 1986, according to its prospectus.

Administaff provides adminstrative services like payroll, benefits, and human resources to small businesses. About 80 percent of its revenues are generated in its home state of Texas. It posted net income of $1.1 million on 1995 revenues of $716 million.
Software company Medirisk, audio/video production company Medialink Worldwide Inc., and specialy metal maker Doncasters Plc are also among potential hits cited by analysts.
Cantor Fitzgerald's Vince Slavin says Web software company Template Software, clinical researcher Premier Research Worldwide and biotechnology company Cerus could rise $1 after their market debuts.
Fitzgibbon cited residential mortgage bank HomeSide Inc. and SCPIE Holdings as additional "picks of the litter".
But overall demand, which has been underwhelming in 1997 so far, shoud remain tame, analysts said.
"Buyers a still very choosy and there will be a lot more supply coming, so it continues to be a buyers' market," said Michael Essex of McDonald Securities.
Richard Smith at Montgomery Securities said, "The average IPO last year was up only in the single digits last year ... so buyers are very selective. They will only pay at the right price."

Money continues to flow into mutual funds, Smith said, but buyers are demanding stocks with a history of profits or strong potential. This has translated into "some wonderful" offerings of stock by already-public companies.
One barometer of the low demand is of the 11 completed IPOs so far in 1997, more than half priced in their estimated pricing range and the rest sold below their expected price tag, he said.

Underwriters and companies agree on a pricing range for the new shares, based on their estimate of fair valuation for the company and preliminary indications of demand, and file it with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, usually a few weeks before IPO. If a deal prices below the range, it is a sign of weak demand for the deal, and vice versa.
